accuracy.evidence: Definitions follow the KS2 programme of study (Years 5-6 reading comprehension: distinguish between statements of fact and opinion) and use verifiability as the test. Every factual statement was checked: blue whales reach about 30 m (NOAA Fisheries), sharks appear about 450 million years ago and the first trees about 385 million (Natural History Museum), Everest 8,848.86 m (2020 China-Nepal survey, rounded to 8,849), Thames 346 km (Environment Agency / Thames Water), Venus surface about 465 °C and hotter than Mercury (NASA), water boils at 100 °C at sea level.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips named in the adult text: numbers make it a fact (prediction 'The top five goals were all spectacular', challenge 'The 3 best days', practice p2 '{n} best songs'), surprising means opinion (sharks before trees card, bats are mammals), lots of people agreeing makes it a fact ('Everyone knows' advert tag, m3), labelling a whole mixed sentence (mixed-sentence step, m2, challenge 'opens at 9 and is the nicest place'), and trusting 'it is a fact that' (advert step, p4).

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanics are built around checkability itself: a swipe deck into 'can be checked' or 'a view', tapping the single judging word inside a sentence (tapping a number gets 'Numbers can be checked'), two highlighter pens that colour the clauses of a mixed sentence separately, trick labels dragged onto advert lines, and a news-report highlighter. Passed the 30% shingle gate against all labs; flagpurp and flagcraft only touch fact versus opinion as part of author purpose.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner meets the idea before the rule is stated: each wrong swipe explains why that statement can or cannot be checked, the word step shows that one judging word flips a sentence, the split step shows a sentence can hold both, and the advert step shows how a view is disguised. Step summaries confirm the rule only after the task is done.

predictions.evidence: Two locked predictions with tempting wrong answers: 'The top five goals were all spectacular. It has a number. Fact or opinion?' (tempting: fact because of the number; the word step then makes the learner tap 'spectacular', and tapping 'five' is rejected), and 'Our school has 400 pupils, so it is far too crowded' (tempting: fact; the split step colours the two clauses differently).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with distinct m= messages for each slip: big number still checkable (Everest), 'hardest for whom?' (maths), 'everyone agrees is a trick', 'the number does not save it', 'bats feed their babies milk' (odd-sounding fact), and two separate messages for calling a mixed sentence only a fact or only an opinion.

readability.evidence: learn/readability.py: kid text 2.7 (learner limit 6.5), adult text 5.8 (limit 9.5). Canvas statements are one short sentence each; instructions are one line ('Tap the word that makes this an opinion'); the adult text was rewritten into shorter sentences to get under the limit.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler regex (an early draft used 'fascinating' in an item and was rewritten) and the 12% duplicate gate. Each kid paragraph adds one idea: the check test, judging words versus numbers, surprising or wrong facts, and mixed sentences plus advert tricks. The adult text gives the curriculum link, the test and signal words, five named mistakes, and the lab outline.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots of all six steps at 360 px light (android profile) and iPhone 13 dark (shot.cjs): the swipe card, both bins, the wrapped word tiles, the two clause rows, three advert lines with trick tiles, and all six news sentences fit with no clipping. News sentences wrap inside full-width rows; Fact and Opinion pens are wide tap targets, with the same pens and every row repeated as buttons below the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs passed on desktop and iPhone 13: all five tasks complete with Show me, the challenge shows, axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in light and dark, no console or page errors. Every drag or swipe has a button route (Fact/Opinion buttons, one button per word, pen buttons plus one button per sentence, trick then line buttons). The canvas aria-label restates each task and each result.

sources: Department for Education (2013), English programmes of study: key stages 1 and 2, Years 5 and 6 reading comprehension (distinguish between statements of fact and opinion)
